description_ru: Эссе о том, почему настоящее извинение стало редкостью, чем оно отличается от пиар-формулы и почему оно требует мужества.
text:
There are two words in the English language that are, for most people, more difficult to pronounce than "otorhinolaryngologist", and they are "I'm sorry." Observe a grown man who has stepped on a stranger's foot on the underground. He will mutter, he will shuffle, he may even produce a small cough that is meant to pass as an apology. What he will not do, if he can possibly avoid it, is to look the injured party in the eye and say the sentence plainly. The apology, it seems, has become the endangered species of public speech, and its disappearance deserves a eulogy.

Public life, in particular, has developed an astonishing repertoire of ways to avoid saying it. We are all familiar with the apology that is not an apology: "I am sorry if anyone was offended," a sentence that cunningly locates the fault in the sensitivities of the audience rather than the conduct of the speaker. Then there is the passive confessional, a masterpiece of evasion, in which "mistakes were made", by nobody in particular, in the way that rain is made. There is the apology for the wrong thing: "I regret that I have been so passionate about my work." And there is the apology that arrives with an appendix: "I'm sorry, but..." in which everything following the word "but" cancels everything that preceded it.

I do not wish to claim that this is a vice peculiar to our time. Humans have always found contrition expensive. But two modern developments have made it more so. The first is the litigious reflex, whereby any acknowledgement of fault is treated by lawyers as an admission that will be used against the client in court. Hospitals, for instance, long advised their physicians never to apologise to patients after an error, and then, to their surprise, discovered that patients who were offered an honest apology were considerably less likely to sue. People, it transpires, are not primarily seeking money. They are seeking recognition.

The second development is the culture of performance. In a world where every utterance may be filmed, quoted and shared, the apology has become a genre of public relations, drafted by committee, rehearsed before a mirror and delivered, with a quivering lip and a carefully chosen tie, in a tone of managed anguish. The viewer, who has seen the genre before, is rarely moved. He interprets the tears as strategy and the sorrow as damage limitation, which in many cases they are. We have thus arrived at a curious paradox: the more elaborately an apology is staged, the less sincere it appears to be.

What, then, makes an apology real? The philosophers and the therapists, who seldom agree on anything, have produced a surprisingly harmonious list. A genuine apology names the offence precisely, without euphemism, so that the injured party can see that it has been understood. It acknowledges the harm done, rather than the harm suffered by the apologiser's reputation. It accepts responsibility without wriggling, and it does not demand forgiveness in return, since forgiveness is a gift and not a transaction. Finally, where possible, it offers some form of repair. A bunch of flowers is not an apology, but a bunch of flowers accompanying an apology is not an insult.

It is worth pausing to ask why the genuine article is so alarming. An apology is, in effect, a voluntary act of self-diminishment. It requires us to concede, in the presence of a witness, that we are not the heroes of our own biographies, and the ego, which prefers to be a patron saint, protests violently. Psychologists speak of cognitive dissonance, the discomfort of holding an idea of oneself as decent and a memory of having behaved badly, and observe that we resolve the tension most readily by revising the memory. The person who has wronged us, we conclude, must have deserved it.

And yet the reward for surmounting this resistance is remarkable. An apology, properly delivered, accomplishes something that almost nothing else can: it alters the past, not literally, of course, but in its meaning. A wound that has been acknowledged heals differently from one that has been denied. The injured party, who has been carrying the grievance as a private burden, is relieved of the exhausting task of persuading the world that it happened. I have witnessed friendships of thirty years' standing, apparently terminal, revive within an afternoon on the strength of a single unadorned sentence.

There is also a benefit to the apologiser, which is rarely advertised. A person who can admit error is, paradoxically, more credible, because his statements about being right are no longer suspect. He has demonstrated that his self-esteem does not depend on being infallible, and that gives him the freedom to learn. The institutions that cultivate such people, the aircraft manufacturers who publish their near-misses, the surgeons who review their blunders in open meetings, are precisely those that improve. Those that conceal their mistakes tend to repeat them with an almost touching fidelity.

Naturally, there are limits. Excessive apology is a different affliction, as anyone who has been to Britain will have noticed, where a person who has been trodden upon will apologise to the shoe. A reflexive "sorry" is a social lubricant, like a handshake, and carries about as much moral weight. Nor should apologies be extracted by force, at the point of a public campaign, since a coerced confession reveals nothing except the efficiency of the coercion. The point is not to have more apologies, but to have fewer occasions that require them, and, when the occasions do arise, to meet them with courage.

I conclude with a small proposal. The next time you find yourself in the wrong, resist the temptation to explain, to qualify, to contextualise or to cite mitigating factors, of which, I assure you, you will find a magnificent supply. Say the sentence. Say it clearly, say it to the person concerned, and then, most difficult of all, stop talking. The silence that follows will feel like a lifetime. It will, in fact, be about two seconds, and it will probably be the most honest two seconds of your week.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Язык не касается нёба, губы слегка округлены; английское r мягче русского «р».
Задняя часть языка касается мягкого нёба, воздух идёт через нос; не добавляйте «г» после ŋ.
Короткий центральный гласный, рот полуоткрыт, губы расслаблены; не заменяйте на русское «о».
Не оглушайте конечные d, b, g: произносите их с голосом, чтобы «bad» не звучало как «bat».

questions.question: What is an apology that is not an apology, according to the author?
questions.answer: One like "I am sorry if anyone was offended".

questions.question: What did hospitals discover about patients who received an honest apology?
questions.answer: They were less likely to sue.

questions.question: What should a genuine apology do?
questions.answer: Name the offence, accept responsibility and offer repair.

questions.question: What is the author's final advice?
questions.answer: Say the sentence clearly and then stop talking.
